passage:
'You're here again?' Pooja asked, finding Irfan on the library steps at lunch.
'Where else? Rehan's lot said the table's full. It's always full.'
'You're still trying to sit with them?'
'I thought if I got good at football...' He shrugged. 'I'm not.'
Pooja pointed at the sketchbook on his knee. 'Is that a kingfisher?'
'Common kingfisher. I saw it at the lake on Sunday. The colours were ridiculous.'
'We've got a bird-count group. Saturdays, six in the morning, by the lake. Four of us and one pair of binoculars we fight over.'
'Six? In the morning?'
'The birds don't wait for you to wake up.' She grinned. 'Bring the sketchbook. Nobody in the group can draw.'
Irfan turned a page. 'I've got a heron too.'
'Then you're definitely coming.'
On Saturday he was at the lake at ten to six.

qa.q: Which bird had Irfan drawn that he saw at the lake on Sunday?
qa.a: He had drawn a common kingfisher, and he had a heron too.

qa.q: What does Irfan's 'I thought if I got good at football...' reveal about how he had been feeling?
qa.a: It shows he had been trying hard to earn a place with Rehan's lot and felt deflated and left out when it didn't work.

qa.q: Why is the bird-count group a better turning point than chasing Rehan's table?
qa.a: It is built around something Irfan already loves, so he can belong by doing and sharing his drawings instead of trying to win over a crowd that keeps saying the table is full.

qa.q: How does Pooja see Irfan's sketchbook?
qa.a: Pooja sees it as something the group is missing, since nobody there can draw, so inviting him feels like gaining a member rather than doing a favour.

grounding: It shows a left-out teen finding belonging in a small group built around a shared interest rather than chasing the popular crowd.

passage:
Last term, when my old group started sitting with the girls from 10B, I spent weeks trying to squeeze back in. I laughed at jokes I didn't get. I bought the same keychain. Nothing changed; I was still the one at the end of the bench.
Then I saw the notice: 'Backstage crew needed for annual play. No acting. Paint, glue, hammers.'
Raghav, who ran it, handed me a brush on the first day and said, 'Vidya, the forest needs more trees.' That was it. No test.
For three weeks we painted, argued about shades of green and ate samosas on dust sheets. Nobody had to be interesting. We just had to finish the forest.
I still see my old group in the corridor. It stings less now. I've got somewhere to be at four.

qa.q: What did the notice say the backstage crew would need?
qa.a: The notice said paint, glue, hammers, and no acting.

qa.q: How did Vidya feel while trying to squeeze back into the old group?
qa.a: Vidya felt left out and anxious to fit in, laughing at jokes that made no sense and buying the same keychain, yet still stuck at the end of the bench.

qa.q: What made the backstage crew work where chasing the old group had not?
qa.a: The crew gathered around a shared task, so belonging came from painting and arguing about green together rather than from having to impress anyone.

qa.q: What might it be like for Raghav to have Vidya join the crew?
qa.a: For Raghav, a new pair of hands means the forest gets more trees; handing over a brush with no test was probably an ordinary, welcome thing to do.

grounding: It shows a teen who was left out finding a place in a backstage crew where belonging grows from doing something together.

passage:
Science teacher's note, Friday
For most of this term Imran, Class 9, has eaten lunch alone near the water tank. I have seen him try to join the cricket group twice; both times they closed ranks, without really meaning to.
Two weeks ago I put up a notice for the new astronomy club, meeting Tuesdays after school. Imran came to the first session and sat at the back. Vinita, from Class 10, was struggling to focus the old telescope. Imran quietly showed her how; he had watched videos about it for months. Since then the two of them have been the first to arrive, arguing happily about Saturn's rings.
Yesterday at lunch I saw him sitting with Vinita and three others from the club, sketching a star chart in a notebook.
Next step: I will ask Imran to help plan our moon-watching night.

qa.q: When does the astronomy club meet?
qa.a: Tuesdays after school.

qa.q: What might Imran have felt showing Vinita how to focus the telescope?
qa.a: He likely felt useful and a little proud, and relieved to be welcomed for something he loves.

qa.q: Why did the astronomy club work where the cricket group didn't?
qa.a: Belonging came from doing a shared interest together, not from trying to win over a closed group.

qa.q: What is it like for Vinita to have Imran in the club?
qa.a: Vinita gains a keen, knowledgeable partner and seems to enjoy their arguments about Saturn's rings.

grounding: A teacher notes how a left-out teen finds belonging in a small club built around a shared interest rather than the popular group.

passage:
Wednesday
Today was the third week of garden club, and I think I actually like it.
Before this I spent every break hanging around the popular boys near the canteen. They'd laugh before I got to the end of my jokes, or just turn their backs. I'd go home feeling like a shadow.
Then Ma'am asked who wanted to help revive the dead vegetable patch behind the library. Only four of us came. Lavanya from 9B knows everything about tomatoes; her grandfather farms. Today we found the first green shoot on the beans, and she screamed so loudly the librarian came out.
Nobody here cares who's cool. We talk about soil and aphids and whose turn it is to water. At lunch Lavanya saved me a spot on the bench.
Tomorrow's my watering day. I've set an alarm.
Jagdish

qa.q: What did the garden club find today?
qa.a: The first green shoot on the beans.

qa.q: How did Jagdish feel going home after trying to join the popular boys?
qa.a: Jagdish felt ignored and small, like a shadow.

qa.q: What helped Jagdish find belonging?
qa.a: Joining a small group around a shared task, the vegetable patch, instead of chasing the popular crowd.

qa.q: What might Lavanya enjoy about the garden club?
qa.a: Lavanya gets to share her farming knowledge with friends who care, and seems happy to save Jagdish a spot.

grounding: A teen stops chasing the popular crowd and finds belonging in a small club built around growing vegetables together.

passage: All of Class 9 in Bhadrachalam seemed to belong to one circle that sat under the neem tree at lunch, and Lavanya had spent a term trying to get into it, laughing at their jokes, buying the same hair clips. It hadn't worked. One Saturday, walking past the old panchayat library, she saw a handwritten sign: "Kolam club. All welcome. Bring chalk." Inside, four people of different ages knelt on the floor around a half-finished pattern. A girl in a green dupatta looked up. "I'm Hafsa. Can you do the curved lines? I always mess them up." Lavanya could, actually; her grandmother had taught her. For two hours nobody asked who she sat with at lunch. They argued about dots and spacing, and Hafsa shared her groundnuts. Walking home with chalk dust on her knees, Lavanya noticed she hadn't once checked what the neem-tree circle was doing.

qa.q: What did the sign outside the panchayat library say to bring?
qa.a: It said to bring chalk.

qa.q: How did Lavanya feel walking home with chalk dust on her knees?
qa.a: She felt content and included, so relaxed that she hadn't once checked on the neem-tree circle.

qa.q: Why did the kolam club work where the neem-tree circle didn't?
qa.a: At the club the shared task gave Lavanya a natural role, since she could draw curved lines, so belonging came from doing something together instead of trying to impress.

qa.q: How might Hafsa see Lavanya after that Saturday?
qa.a: Hafsa may be glad to have found someone who can do the curved lines and hope Lavanya comes back.

grounding: Shows a left-out teen finding belonging in a small group built around a shared interest instead of chasing the popular crowd.
